item.title: Cervical — Mulligan Mobilization With Movement (MWM) Clinical Guidance
clinicalUse: Mulligan Mobilization With Movement (MWM) is not routinely a first-choice application for Cervical.
Use it only when examination identifies a relevant target, the clinician is appropriately trained and a safer/more direct option is not preferable.
The treatment decision must still be based on the patient's comparable sign: neck pain, cervical range, headache-related comparable signs and upper-limb symptom behavior.
patientPosition: Use supported sitting, supine or prone according to the technique and irritability.
Keep the head and shoulders relaxed and avoid unnecessary end-range positioning.
therapistPosition: Work close to the patient with the head/neck fully controlled.
Use relaxed shoulders and low force before considering progression.
stabilization: Control adjacent cervical segments and the shoulder girdle so the intended target is not replaced by global neck motion.
contact: Do not force a textbook contact simply to make this technique fit the region.
Apply the accessory glide that makes the patient's active movement easier or pain-free.
A belt may be used only where trained and where it improves control.
forceDirection: Maintain the accessory glide while the patient performs the comparable active movement.
The direction is modified until the movement shows an immediate acceptable improvement.
dosage: Often 6–10 repetitions for 2–3 sets when the response stays pain-free and useful.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Cervical: neck pain, cervical range, headache-related comparable signs and upper-limb symptom behavior.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Confirm that this technique is genuinely relevant to the identified target; if not, choose a more appropriate regional technique.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Screen fracture/instability, progressive neurological deficit, myelopathy and vascular warning features before cervical manual therapy.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Cervical assessment → correct regional setup → Mobilization With Movement → immediate comparable-sign re-test.
